title: Community Engagement: Listening with Purpose and Respect
audience: All staff, including supervisors and managers

slides.text:
One DSD People, Access and Culture
Community Engagement: Listening with Purpose and Respect
Invite useful perspectives, explain their influence, and return an honest account of what happened to the input.
Foundation self-directed learning
slides.narration: Community engagement brings knowledge into public work that staff cannot supply alone. Its value depends on more than asking people to attend or counting comments. People need to understand the question, use the participation route, and know what their contribution can influence. This course uses service, workplace, and community examples to practice those distinctions. You will consider timing, decision boundaries, and follow-through while preserving people’s choice and the actual responsibilities of those making the decision.

slides.text:
What was still open when people were asked?
A team requests feedback after choosing the approach. Participants suggest alternatives that staff cannot consider.

The invitation may be sincere while its promised influence is unclear.

What could staff explain before asking people to spend their time?
slides.narration: A request for feedback can sound open even when the meaningful choice has already been made. Participants may then invest effort in questions the team cannot act on. That does not mean informing people about a settled decision is wrong. It means the purpose should be named accurately. Repeating ambiguous invitations may make participation feel like endorsement rather than influence. Consider what is actually open and how to explain it, without assuming that every limit makes the conversation useless.

slides.text:
Information, input, and shared work differ
Informing explains a decision. Seeking input invites knowledge that may shape a decision held by the responsible role.

Working through options together shares more of the reasoning and influence.

Name the actual arrangement; none should promise authority it does not provide.
slides.narration: Different participation arrangements can serve legitimate purposes. A settled requirement may need an understandable explanation, while an open design question can benefit from input. Working through options together may offer a deeper role in the reasoning. The important distinction is what people can influence and who retains the decision. Do not call every conversation co-design or treat information as if it offered control. A clear invitation respects the person’s time and helps their contribution fit the actual task.

slides.text:
A nearly final service notice
A team invites comments on a service notice after choosing its approach. Wording can still change, but the underlying rule is not open in that review.

An unclear invitation can direct effort toward unavailable choices.

Explain the scope and hear related concerns without pretending they are already resolved.
slides.narration: The wording review can still be useful if participants know its boundaries. They may identify a confusing instruction or missing next step. A concern about the underlying rule may need a different appropriate route, and it should not be dismissed simply because this review cannot decide it. The next case asks how to make that distinction honest. The fiction supplies no actual rule, review authority, or release decision. It prepares a clearer invitation rather than establishing a new engagement procedure.

slides.text:
A wording review with honest boundaries
A service notice is nearly final. Wording can change, but the underlying rule is outside this review. What should the invitation say?
A. Invite people to redesign the whole service without mentioning limits.
B. Explain the wording question and boundary, with appropriate routes for related concerns to clarify.
C. Cancel all feedback because no useful influence is possible.
In Slide Show view, select a response to explore its effects.
slides.narration: The review has a real but bounded opportunity. Wording can affect what people understand and do, even when the underlying rule is not open here. Participants should know that before choosing to spend time. A related concern should not be treated as irrelevant, but its appropriate route needs clarification. Compare invitations that promise too much or abandon listening with an invitation that names the actual scope. The fiction supplies no working contact or approved release. It prepares an honest explanation and leaves participation arrangements and later results open.

links.name: Answer 1
links.text: A. Invite people to redesign the whole service without mentioning limits.

links.name: Answer 2
links.text: B. Explain the wording question and boundary, with appropriate routes for related concerns to clarify.

links.name: Answer 3
links.text: C. Cancel all feedback because no useful influence is possible.

slides.text:
Consider the possible effects
The promise exceeds the open choice. Repetition can ask people to spend effort on unavailable changes. Explain scope honestly; authority over the rule and a complete participation route are not supplied.

What choice can the participant influence in this review?
Continue learning
Try another response
slides.narration: Promising complete redesign may sound inclusive while directing effort toward choices this review cannot make. If repeated, people may experience engagement as a request to endorse a settled approach. Explain what is actually open and how other concerns can be considered appropriately. The case does not supply authority over the service rule or a functioning route for those broader decisions.

slides.text:
Why this response helps
This respects time and makes the actual influence visible. It may reduce a recurring gap between invitation and consideration. Clarify usable arrangements and other routes; no participation or accepted change is yet known.

What choice can the participant influence in this review?
Try another response
Continue learning
slides.narration: The invitation connects the person’s contribution with the actual question and states the limit. That can make feedback more useful without dismissing concerns outside the scope. Appropriate participation arrangements and related routes still need clarification. The response is a supported draft, not a completed session, adopted wording, or proof that people found the influence meaningful.

slides.text:
Consider the possible effects
A wording review may still improve usable information. Dismissing it loses a possible contribution. Invite the open question honestly; its value and wider effects still need evidence.

What choice can the participant influence in this review?
Try another response
Continue learning
slides.narration: The open wording question may affect usability, so canceling all feedback assumes no value without examining it. People can identify unclear instructions even within a bounded review. Offer an honest scope and appropriate ways to contribute. The case does not guarantee that any suggestion will be adopted or that wording alone resolves the broader concern, but those limits do not erase possible influence.

slides.text:
Ask a question people can answer
A useful invitation names the issue, the material to consider, and the purpose of the input.

“What do you think?” may leave the actual task unclear.

Invite relevant knowledge without requiring a whole personal history.
slides.narration: A broad question can welcome conversation, but it may not help people decide what information is useful. If the task concerns a notice’s next step, say that and identify the passage. Participants can then offer what they notice without recounting every service experience. This specificity should not silence an unexpected concern; it makes the starting purpose understandable. Repeatedly requiring broad personal explanations can burden participation and obscure the practical contribution. Keep the inquiry open enough to learn while respecting information boundaries.

slides.text:
Meaningful presence depends on a usable route
Timing, language, disability access, materials, and response methods affect who can contribute.

An invitation sent is not proof that it could be used.

Consider the connected steps before interpreting absent voices.
slides.narration: Participation begins with reaching and understanding the opportunity. An inaccessible attachment or an unavailable registration route can exclude a person before the session starts. During the discussion, pace and response methods shape whose contribution becomes visible. Examine those conditions through the appropriate responsibilities rather than assuming a community’s preferences. Repetition can make the same voices easiest to hear. A more usable route may broaden participation, but the invitation itself does not establish attendance, representation, or meaningful influence.

slides.text:
People can decline without supplying a reason
Voluntary contribution leaves room to say no, pause, or choose a limited account.

Absence does not establish agreement, distrust, disinterest, or a particular barrier.

Ask proportionate questions where appropriate and retain what remains unknown.
slides.narration: A person may decline for reasons that are private or simply not available to staff. Treating that choice as evidence of a community’s attitude would go beyond the information. It also should not remove the person’s rights or future opportunity. An appropriate review can ask whether the participation route was usable without requiring an explanation from everyone who did not attend. Keep missing perspectives visible. The point is to learn about the arrangement, not make participation a test of loyalty or gratitude.

slides.text:
Input can challenge the staff interpretation
A question about timing may express preparation rather than impatience. A question about use may express care for one’s contribution rather than reluctance.

Ask what the concern means before applying a label.

A different meaning can change the response.
slides.narration: Staff may interpret a request through their own learned expectations. Someone asking how input will be used might be trying to understand responsibility for their words, not resisting the task. Someone asking early may want to prepare carefully. Hear the particular account when offered and let it refine the interpretation. Do not infer a group style from it. Repeating dismissive labels can make useful concerns less credible, while understanding meaning can help staff respond to the actual question.

slides.text:
Employee feedback after a choice is made
A supervisor asks employees to shape onboarding after choosing the next approach. Only parts of the materials can still change.

The promise may exceed the real influence.

Explain the open parts and appropriate ways to raise other concerns.
slides.narration: The workplace example applies the same participation principle within actual supervision. Employees may have useful knowledge from onboarding, but the scope of this review matters. If the approach is settled, staff should not imply that every suggested alternative can determine it. Materials or implementation questions may remain open, and other concerns may need another route. The next choice asks how to invite input honestly without abandoning the value of listening. The fiction supplies no new supervisory mandate or agreed change.

slides.text:
An onboarding invitation after the approach is chosen
A supervisor asks staff to shape onboarding after choosing the approach. Only parts of the materials remain open. What response best makes the participation honest?
A. Name the open material questions, explain the settled part, and hear other concerns at their appropriate scope.
B. Tell employees that any suggestion will determine the approach.
C. Treat every employee who questions the boundary as resistant.
In Slide Show view, select a response to explore its effects.
slides.narration: Employee feedback can improve materials while another part of the approach remains settled. The invitation should make that distinction clear rather than imply unlimited influence. Staff may also raise an issue outside the material review, which can be heard without claiming this conversation decides it. Consider which response preserves practical knowledge and actual responsibility together. The fiction does not establish employee motives, a new supervisory process, or an adopted revision. Its purpose is to practice an honest invitation within the relevant employee life-cycle experience.

links.name: Answer 1
links.text: A. Name the open material questions, explain the settled part, and hear other concerns at their appropriate scope.

links.name: Answer 2
links.text: B. Tell employees that any suggestion will determine the approach.

links.name: Answer 3
links.text: C. Treat every employee who questions the boundary as resistant.

slides.text:
Why this response helps
This makes input and actual influence fit together. It may interrupt a recurring promise that exceeds the review. Clarify usable contribution and other routes; agreement and later effects remain unknown.

How would you invite useful employee knowledge without overstating control?
Try another response
Continue learning
slides.narration: The response tells employees where their knowledge can affect the work. It also leaves room to hear broader concerns without promising this review can decide them. If repeated, such clarity may reduce the gap between being asked and being able to influence. Usable arrangements, actual routes, and later consideration still need attention. No agreement, adopted material, or improved onboarding result is supplied.

slides.text:
Consider the possible effects
The promise is not supported by the settled choice. Repetition may create misleading expectations. Explain the actual scope and responsibilities; the case supplies no authority to reopen every part.

How would you invite useful employee knowledge without overstating control?
Continue learning
Try another response
slides.narration: Telling staff every suggestion will determine the approach conflicts with the stated boundary. People may spend effort expecting authority the review does not offer. Repeating that promise can make later limits feel like disregard for input. Explain the open questions and actual roles honestly. The case supplies no reopened decision or authority to let the invitation settle every part.

slides.text:
Consider the possible effects
The label can discount useful employee knowledge and weaken voice. Repetition may leave onboarding gaps unexamined. Hear the concern and explain the boundary; motives are unknown.

How would you invite useful employee knowledge without overstating control?
Try another response
Continue learning
slides.narration: Questioning a boundary can express a need to understand influence rather than resistance. A label may make that inquiry less credible and leave useful onboarding knowledge unheard. If repeated, employee participation can become conditional on agreement. Receive the question and explain what is open, while preserving appropriate other routes. The fiction does not establish a motive or a capability judgment about any employee.

slides.text:
Workplace voice runs through the life cycle
Recruitment, onboarding, feedback, development, and transitions can reveal different aspects of the employee experience.

Invite the knowledge relevant to the question, using appropriate arrangements.

Do not make an employee speak for everyone who shares an identity or role.
slides.narration: An onboarding account can reveal what a newcomer needed to understand; a development account may concern a different opportunity route. Match the inquiry to the stage rather than assuming one question captures the whole employee life cycle. Employees may choose how much to offer, and formal processes retain their responsibilities. A repeated expectation that one person represents an identity or job category can burden them and hide variation. Listening should make practical knowledge easier to consider, not assign an unrequested representative role.

slides.text:
Hearing is not the same as agreeing
A concern can be received accurately even when a proposed solution cannot be adopted.

Explain the relevant limit and consider what the information does help clarify.

Do not use disagreement as a reason to erase the account.
slides.narration: Staff remain responsible for weighing evidence, requirements, and alternatives. Listening does not require accepting every proposal, but it does require understanding what was offered. A participant may identify a real burden while suggesting an option outside the available authority. The account can still inform another response or an appropriate next question. Repeatedly equating inability to adopt a proposal with lack of value can narrow engagement. Return an honest explanation of the consideration and limits, without claiming the person agreed with the final choice.

slides.text:
Briefs prepare a respectful starting point
Community briefs can introduce context, institutions, and questions staff might otherwise miss.

Current, varied perspectives remain necessary for the actual issue.

Preparation should reduce assumptions rather than become a description imposed on each participant.
slides.narration: A brief can help staff enter a conversation with awareness of history and institutional experience. It cannot tell them what this person wants from the review or how the invitation will be received. Use the background to form open questions and seek varied perspectives. If the brief becomes the assumed answer, engagement may merely confirm a profile. The person’s chosen account remains their own. Native American and Tribal-specific matters follow the appropriate ADSA office referral rather than being authored or generalized in this course.

slides.text:
One partner brings knowledge, not everyone
A familiar community partner may hold valuable expertise and relationships.

That contribution does not establish the views of all people affected.

Ask which perspectives remain missing and how relevant participation can be broadened.
slides.narration: Working with a trusted partner can make engagement more informed. The partner’s reach still has boundaries, and other people may have different experiences or not be connected to the same network. Ask respectfully what the contribution concerns and which questions need additional knowledge. Repeatedly relying on one partner as the entire community can make its perspective the default. Do not replace that shortcut by demanding impossible completeness. Seek a proportionate range of relevant perspectives and state the remaining limits honestly.

slides.text:
A familiar partner is treated as the whole community
One partner comments on an access question. Staff propose reporting that “the community supports the plan.”

The wording enlarges a specific contribution into agreement not supplied.

Keep the account’s scope and seek other relevant perspectives before making a broader claim.
slides.narration: The partner may support a feature, question another part, or offer knowledge without endorsing the plan. A broad statement of community agreement can erase those distinctions. If repeated, the organization may use one familiar relationship as evidence that missing voices were considered. The next choice asks how to report the contribution accurately. The fiction supplies no representative authorization, complete range of views, or accepted plan. It supports a more honest account that preserves useful knowledge and the perspectives still absent.

slides.text:
One partner’s contribution and a wider claim
A familiar partner comments on one access issue. Staff propose saying “the community supports the plan.” Which account is most accurate?
A. The partner’s identity establishes authority to speak for everyone.
B. No useful community knowledge exists until every person participates.
C. Describe the particular contribution, its influence, and perspectives still missing without claiming universal support.
In Slide Show view, select a response to explore its effects.
slides.narration: The partner can offer valuable knowledge without endorsing every part of the plan or representing everyone affected. A broad support statement may erase the contribution’s scope and the voices still absent. Consider how to report the knowledge and its influence accurately. Community briefs can prepare questions about missing perspectives but cannot supply agreement. The fiction contains no representative mandate or completed decision. A careful account can recognize the partner’s expertise and identify the next relevant inquiry without requiring impossible completeness or making an unsupported universal claim.

links.name: Answer 1
links.text: A. The partner’s identity establishes authority to speak for everyone.

links.name: Answer 2
links.text: B. No useful community knowledge exists until every person participates.

links.name: Answer 3
links.text: C. Describe the particular contribution, its influence, and perspectives still missing without claiming universal support.

slides.text:
Consider the possible effects
Identity does not establish representative authority or agreement. Repetition can turn one voice into an institutional shortcut. Keep the account’s scope and seek relevant perspectives; broader support is unknown.

What statement would preserve the partner’s actual contribution?
Try another response
Continue learning
slides.narration: A shared identity or familiar partnership does not automatically confer authority to speak for every community member. Treating it that way can make one account the default in future decisions while other experiences remain unheard. Describe what was actually offered and ask about relevant representative scope when appropriate. The case does not supply endorsement of the whole plan, representative authorization, or universal agreement.

slides.text:
Consider the possible effects
Completeness is not required for a useful account. Dismissing the contribution loses knowledge. Retain it accurately while examining missing perspectives; no complete community view is supplied.

What statement would preserve the partner’s actual contribution?
Try another response
Continue learning
slides.narration: No engagement can promise to hear every person, and that limit does not make a particular contribution useless. Dismissing it sacrifices knowledge rather than improving representation. Retain the account and identify missing perspectives proportionate to the issue. Appropriate additional participation may deepen the understanding. The fiction supplies one useful contribution, not a complete community view or evidence that no further inquiry matters.

slides.text:
Why this response helps
This values the contribution without enlarging its evidence. It may reduce a recurring representation gap. Explain actual consideration and limits; wider agreement and the final decision remain open.

What statement would preserve the partner’s actual contribution?
Continue learning
Try another response
slides.narration: The account preserves expertise and its limits together. It can show which question the input informed and what remains absent without claiming everyone supports the plan. If maintained, that discipline may reduce reliance on one familiar voice as universal evidence. The actual decision and wider agreement remain open. Returning the honest account also requires appropriate information handling rather than unnecessary identification of the contributor.

slides.text:
Trace a concern into the reasoning
Record the specific question it informed, not only the number of comments.

Distinguish a wording proposal, a fact needing confirmation, and a decision beyond this review.

Use appropriate information handling and avoid publishing personal accounts unnecessarily.
slides.narration: A summary saying people wanted better communication may lose the practical issue. One person may ask when a question can be raised, while another asks whether asking starts an application. Those concerns need different answers. Trace each into the reasoning at an appropriate level. The account should not identify people unnecessarily or imply a commitment not established. This makes input visible as knowledge rather than a decorative attendance measure, while actual facts, decisions, and information arrangements remain appropriately governed.

slides.text:
Return what happened to the input
Explain what was considered, what changed or is proposed, what could not change, and which questions remain.

Do not report adoption where only a recommendation exists.

An honest return can respect a contribution without promising satisfaction or agreement.
slides.narration: Closing the loop means showing how the input relates to the actual work. If a recommendation was drafted but not adopted, say that. If a limit prevented a change, explain it in useful terms rather than a vague dismissal. A participant may still disagree or want another route. Returning the account does not guarantee trust or satisfaction, but it makes the organization’s reasoning more visible. Repeatedly collecting input without such a return can leave people unsure whether their knowledge had any place in the decision.

slides.text:
Rewrite an invitation with honest influence
Use the notice or onboarding fiction.

Name the open question, real boundary, usable participation route to clarify, and how input would be returned.

Do not invent a working contact, timetable, or commitment.
slides.narration: Write the invitation as something a person could understand before deciding whether to contribute. Explain that the review concerns wording if that is the open choice, and identify the other concern as needing its appropriate route. You can state what still requires clarification without inventing a receiver or guaranteed method. Your reflection can stay private. The purpose is a truthful relationship between the invitation and influence, not a new procedure or a claim that every participant will accept the arrangement.

slides.text:
Look at influence as well as participation counts
Attendance and comments describe activity. The decision account helps show how knowledge was considered.

Ask what people could influence and which perspectives remain missing.

A count alone does not establish meaningful participation or a complete community view.
slides.narration: A session with many attendees can still leave the main choice unavailable, while a smaller focused review can provide valuable knowledge. Numbers help describe the activity but do not settle the quality of influence. Examine the invitation, timing, actual consideration, and returned account. Keep the limits of representation visible. Do not turn no reply into agreement or demand positive feedback to certify the effort. A useful review recognizes what engagement contributed and what the current information cannot establish.

slides.text:
Listen in a way that people can recognize
Purpose, usable participation, honest influence, and an accurate return make engagement more meaningful.

Value specific knowledge without assigning a whole community to one person.

Continue with community briefs, accessibility, and equity review when they deepen the actual question.
slides.narration: Respectful engagement is a relationship between the question offered, the conditions of participation, and what happens to the contribution. The cases show how an unclear boundary or enlarged claim can make sincere listening less useful. Keep people’s choice and actual decision responsibilities visible. Preparation helps you ask better questions, while varied accounts improve what staff understand. An honest return can recognize the input even when a proposal is not adopted. Continued learning should support that relationship rather than treat participation as a box already checked.

outcomes: Distinguish informing, seeking input, and sharing influence over a decision.
Explain what is open to change before asking people to participate.
Identify barriers to being present and contributing meaningfully.
Describe how to return an honest account of what happened to people’s input.
